summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national framework has recently moved against trans people's access to public space. On 2 April 2025 the Plenary of Congress approved, exempt from a second vote, the fused bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, later promulgated as the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents. Article 5 of the text prohibits entry to and use of public sanitary facilities by any person whose biological sex does not match the sex for which the facility is designated, with listed exceptions. The provision passed after a February 2025 approval, unanimously, by the Women and Family Commission on the Muñante initiative, and it also bars inclusive signage of the kind the international airport in Lima had installed, signage reading "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity".

IDEHPUCP, the human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, published an analysis of the rule on 15 April 2025 by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte. They describe it as direct legislation conditioning basic rights on "biological sex" and as a violation of the equality and non-discrimination principle, and note that trans people, though the rule frames them as aggressors, are more often the victims of violence and discrimination. LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho, quoted on the February 2025 approval, called the measure discriminatory and described what enforcement would amount to in practice: security staff deciding on their own judgement whether a woman entering a restroom is trans, and demanding her national identity document (DNI).

That enforcement mechanism reaches private business and public life in Lima. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that applied the policy. On television, Willax TV presenter Ana María Salcedo publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to go use the men's room. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Violence against trans people in Peru is documented and, on its own figures, under-recorded. The TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report, published by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, recorded 54 murders of LGBTI people and 170 reports of rights violations between 2020 and 2023. More than half of the dead were trans women (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. 2023 was the year with the most homicides, 19, and in 26 of the 54 killings no suspects were identified. In central Lima, on 12 February 2023, the "Los Gallegos" extortion gang abducted the transgender sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, from jirón Chancay and killed her with roughly 30 gunshots. The report flags state inaction: no official system records victims' sexual orientation, and hate crimes go unsanctioned. Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender and a co-author of the 2024 hate-crime research, has stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

Two convictions and one legal reversal sit alongside the violence record. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly twenty years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, according to BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights. In July 2025 a constitutional court in Lima, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

The country's protections were weakened on paper well before the bathroom law. In 2017 Peru's Congress voted to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. The April 2025 law also constrains speech and association: vague child-protection articles, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
Hate crime is a documented trend, not an isolated episode. The 2024 observatory figures show 54 killings and 170 rights-violation reports over four years, with the highest single-year homicide count in 2023 and no identified suspects in nearly half the cases. The trend is national and trans women bear the largest share.

Peru's position on the regional map of protection is unusually poor. After the 2017 repeal it joined Paraguay and Guyana as the only South American jurisdictions without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law, while the Inter-American Court has, in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 and the Rojas Marín case, established regional standards that the domestic statute no longer reflects.

Protective developments are partial and come from outside Congress. Health guidance for trans patients was de-pathologised in June 2024, and a Lima constitutional court struck down an anti-equality decree in July 2025 after activist litigation. Neither offsets the April 2025 statutory restriction or the repeal of hate-crime coverage.
localsOnly:
Residents face the bathroom rule in ordinary settings: schools, shopping centres, offices, the international airport's facilities, and gyms that have adopted it. Enforcement rests on security staff acting on appearance, backed by demands for the DNI. The same norm extends to signage, so inclusive wording on facility doors is itself prohibited.

Access to healthcare improved on paper in June 2024 when the health ministry removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official guidance. In practice the same period records violence against trans residents and, for residents, an observatory that compiles killings and rights violations in the absence of any official state system recording sexual orientation.

For residents, the hate-crime gap is structural: the Penal Code's 2017 repeal removed LGBT anti-discrimination coverage, so prosecutors have no hate-crime charge to bring. The Rojas Marín ruling, first in the country and first torture-by-discrimination case before the Inter-American Court, shows the route that does work, through the Inter-American Commission and years of litigation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state how the April 2025 article 5 rule is being administered in Lima's municipal or state facilities, how many complaints have been filed or dismissed under it, or whether any Lima business besides the gym named here has been reported enforcing it.

Whether the July 2025 ruling by the Lima constitutional court is directly connected to trans rights or to a broader equality principle is not specified in the sources available. The "anti-equality decree" is named in neither the visible sources nor the claim inventory.

No figure is available for the number of trans people killed in Lima specifically between 2020 and 2023; the observatory counts are national. The 54-killings figure also appears in the parent framework as "transgender and gender-diverse people" rather than as LGBTI people overall, and the two framings have not been reconciled here.

No source reports trans people being refused entry to Peru or subjected to border screening on the basis of gender identity or documentation mismatch. Entry and visa treatment is not evidenced in this inventory.
